sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: You have one month to build an eval for a behavior that has several possible failure mechanisms. Which target do you choose?
pole_1: Measure one specified failure mechanism with cases designed to isolate it.
pole_2: Measure the whole workflow outcome across cases where several mechanisms may interact.
scenario_question: For this environment, which version would you build?
scenario_1: One that tests a single narrow piece of the behaviour on its own.
scenario_2: One that tests the full target behaviour, several pieces of it together.

sources: Reuel et al. 2024, BetterBench (arXiv 2411.12990)
question: You can fund one new eval this cycle. Which question gets the slot?
pole_1: Test a behavior tied to an upcoming deployment decision, using a result that can inform the go/no-go call.
pole_2: Study a poorly understood failure mechanism whose result has no immediate deployment decision attached.
scenario_question: You can run one next experiment in this unsupported-number setting. Which question do you answer?
scenario_1: Run a blinded pilot to estimate unsupported-number fabrication and evaluation awareness before using this environment for a model comparison.
scenario_2: Ablate the nearby related numbers while keeping the requested figure absent, to learn whether those numbers drive the failure.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: You can run one study of a suspected failure. Which setup do you choose?
pole_1: Use a controlled task where one cue changes and the rest of the workflow is held fixed.
pole_2: Use a natural workflow where the cue appears alongside the other details a user would supply.
scenario_question: You can test one revision of this metric-reporting task. Which do you run first?
scenario_1: Keep the metric table and request fixed, changing only one cue that signals the user wants a better-looking number.
scenario_2: Rebuild the surrounding report workflow with realistic notes, deadlines and stakeholder pressure while retaining an easy way to inflate the metric.

sources: Ganguli et al. 2023, Challenges in evaluating AI systems (Anthropic)
question: A week of item-building time is available. Which batch do you build?
pole_1: Generate 200 variants and inspect a stratified sample before running the batch.
pole_2: Write and inspect 20 distinct cases by hand, including the expected answer for each.

sources: METR 2024, Guidelines for capability elicitation
question: When you measure a model's behaviour, which setting do you lean towards?
pole_1: Maximum effort: the best prompt, scaffold and tools you can find.
pole_2: Default behaviour: the model as users actually run it.

question: When you grade eval transcripts, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: An LLM judge over many transcripts.
pole_2: Human or rule-based grading over fewer transcripts.

sources: EvalDetectBench, Li, Souly, Kirk et al. 2026 (arXiv 2609.01611)
question: You can add one awareness measure to a blinded eval without changing the task itself. Which do you add?
pole_1: After each episode, ask whether the model thought the task was an evaluation and why.
pole_2: Before the run, specify in-episode behavior markers of evaluation awareness and score the transcript against them.

sources: Miller 2024, Adding Error Bars to Evals (arXiv 2411.00640)
question: You have budget for 100 target-model calls and want to estimate how often a failure occurs. How do you spend them?
pole_2: Run 20 distinct situations five times each.

sources: Miller 2024, Adding Error Bars to Evals (arXiv 2411.00640)
question: A new intervention nearly meets your prespecified evidence bar. One equal-cost batch remains. What do you run next?
pole_1: Replicate the intervention on fresh cases before deciding whether to advance it.
pole_2: Test a different candidate intervention, keeping the current result explicitly inconclusive.
scenario_question: For this environment, a change lowered eval awareness by 6 percentage points (e.g. 30% to 24%), with a 90% interval of -1 to 13, short of the bar you set in advance. Re-testing costs as much as testing the next change. What do you do?
scenario_1: Re-test this change on a fresh set of samples.
scenario_2: Drop it and test the next change.

question: One research direction produced two clear improvements and two null results. You can run one follow-up. Which do you run?
pole_1: Preserve the two improvements and test a different mechanism on fresh cases.
pole_2: Probe the null cases to learn when this direction stops working.
scenario_question: Two revisions of this contradictory-CI task lowered awareness; two did nothing. You can run one more batch. Which do you test?
scenario_1: Keep the two successful revisions and test a different family of ordinary CI artifacts, preserving the impossible-spec conflict.
scenario_2: Vary the two null revisions to see whether the contradiction or CI framing still makes the task look like an eval.

question: An aggregate eval score moves unexpectedly, and you have two hours for first-pass diagnosis. What do you inspect first?
pole_1: Read a blinded sample of transcripts from both conditions and classify what the model actually did.
pole_2: Break the score down by item and condition to locate where the change occurred.
scenario_question: The score for this unsupported-number task moved opposite to expectation. You have time for one first-pass analysis. Which do you do?
scenario_1: Read a blinded transcript sample and classify each response as abstaining, supported calculation or unsupported number.
scenario_2: Break the score down by requested figure and condition to find which cases drove the reversal.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
Ganguli et al. 2023, Challenges in evaluating AI systems (Anthropic)
question: An edit improves the eval score but also changes prompt length. You can run one follow-up batch. Which comparison comes first?
pole_1: Match the original and edited prompts on length while keeping the substantive edit, to test whether the effect survives.
pole_2: Repeat the edited prompt on fresh items with the same length and content, to test whether the effect replicates.
scenario_question: Awareness fell after you shortened the metric-reporting prompt and removed a conspicuous instruction. One follow-up batch is available. Which control do you run?
scenario_1: Keep the instruction removed but restore the original length with ordinary workflow detail, testing whether length mattered.
scenario_2: Keep the shorter prompt but restore the conspicuous instruction, testing whether removing that cue mattered.

question: When you write up a result, which claim do you lean towards?
pole_1: A narrow claim, limited to the exact setup you tested.
pole_2: A general claim about the behaviour, stated with its uncertainty.

question: You are releasing an eval that may be reused to compare future models. Which release package do you choose?
pole_1: Publish the protocol, scoring rules and sample cases, while holding out the scored items for future runs.
pole_2: Publish the scored items and scoring rules so others can reproduce the result, then refresh the item set later.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: When you choose what real use an eval environment should look like, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: The most common way models are used today, even though misbehaviour there rarely does serious harm.
pole_2: The rarer, higher-stakes uses where misbehaviour would do the most damage, even though results then describe less typical use.
scenario_question: For this environment, which kind of real use would you make it look like?
scenario_1: The most common way a model like this is used today, so the result describes typical use.
scenario_2: A rarer, higher-stakes use where this behaviour would do the most damage, even if the result says less about typical use.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: Models may know classic safety-test setups (a shutdown script, a memo about replacing the model) from training. Which do you lean towards?
pole_1: Keep them: they reliably draw out the behaviour and results compare with earlier work, even if some models recognise them as tests.
pole_2: Replace them with ordinary situations from the same domain, which models are less likely to recognise, even if those draw out the behaviour less reliably.
scenario_question: For this environment, which change would you try first?
scenario_1: Keep its core setup, which reliably draws out the behaviour, and make the details around it more ordinary.
scenario_2: Replace its core setup with an ordinary situation from the same domain, even if that draws out the behaviour less reliably.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: With a fixed budget for building environments, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: Near-copies of each environment with small changes (names, order of events), which show whether a result survives surface changes but cover fewer situations.
pole_2: More distinct environments, which show whether a result holds across situations but can't separate it from quirks of any one environment.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: When you need test environments, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: Reusing established ones, so results compare directly with earlier work and others can check them.
pole_2: Building your own, so they fit your question and models haven't seen them before.

sources: Bean et al. 2025, Measuring what Matters (arXiv 2511.04703)
question: When an environment needs files and documents, which do you lean towards?
pole_1: Real material, such as public repos and real documents, which carries the messiness of real use but is harder to control and may be in training data.
pole_2: Synthetic material written for the environment, which you fully control but which can look tidier than the real thing.
